                      fig.retina = 2, message = FALSE)
project <- normalizePath("../../examples/oppeltNPJSystBiolAppl2018")

knitr::read_chunk("../../examples/oppeltNPJSystBiolAppl2018/sensitivities.R")

```{r, echo = FALSE}
s <- stored("results/sensitivities.rds", "sensitivities.R")
```

Fits, profiles and mixed-effects models need derivatives of the objective. dMod2 computes them
exactly from the ODE sensitivities, propagated by the chain rule through every function object,
without finite differences. This chapter covers forward, forward over forward, reverse and forward
over reverse, the backends of `odemodel()`, and their costs on the guide model (`sensitivities.R`
of the project). Details: [Methods > Sensitivities and Hessians](methods-sensitivities.html).

## Forward sensitivities

The default. `Xs()` integrates the sensitivities $\partial x / \partial \theta$ with the states,
and every function object of `g*x*p` multiplies them by the Jacobian of that object. The objective returns
gradient and Gauss-Newton Hessian for one solve with a tangent per parameter. `sensErrCon` in
`optionsSens` of `Xs()` sets whether sensitivities enter the error test, by default yes. With fixed
standard deviations the Gauss-Newton Hessian is positive semidefinite, with an error model it can
be indefinite
([Methods > Gauss-Newton with an error model](methods-sensitivities.html#gauss-newton-with-an-error-model)).

## Forward over forward

`deriv2 = TRUE` in `odemodel()`, `Y()`, `P()` and `Pimpl()` builds second-order sensitivities; the objective
called with `deriv2 = TRUE` and the forward sweep returns the exact Hessian. The equation count
grows with the square of the parameters, so this suits small models such as those of
[Nonlinear mixed-effects models](guide-nlme.html). The guide model with
`r nrow(s$gradients)`
parameters uses it once below to show the cost.

## Reverse sweep

The gradient alone comes from one backward sweep of the adjoint system, at a cost independent of
the parameter count
([Methods > Reverse sweep](methods-sensitivities.html#reverse-sweep)). Every function object but
`Pimpl()`, which passes the sweep through the Jacobian of the root, is built with
`derivMode = c("forward", "reverse")`, and the model is called with `sweep = "reverse"`. Both
passes use the solver `options` alone; solves with sensitivities use `optionsSens` merged over
`options`.

In `trust()` the sweep is set per phase:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
fit <- trust(obj, start,
             phases = list(list(hessianMethod = "gn"),
                           list(hessianMethod = "sr1", sweep = "reverse")))
fit$phaseSweep
```

Without `sweep`, `"bfgs"` and `"sr1"` phases sweep backwards if the objective allows it at the
start, otherwise forwards. Gauss-Newton always runs forwards, since $J^\top J$ needs forward
sensitivities; a `"gn"` phase with `sweep = "reverse"` is an error, and the objective called with
`sweep = "reverse"` returns no Gauss-Newton Hessian, with a warning where `hessian = TRUE` asks for
one. `"exact"` runs
forwards by default and backwards with `sweep = "reverse"`, where `deriv2 = TRUE` gives the exact
Hessian by forward over reverse. A change of sweep between phases evaluates the current iterate
once more. [Optimization](guide-optimization.html) compares the Hessian sources on the guide model.

The backward sweep follows the step grid of the value pass by default. On the cppDE backend,
`optionsReverse` of `Xs()` sets the accuracy, see `cppDE::adjointControl()`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
x <- Xs(model, options = list(atol = 1e-8, rtol = 1e-6),
        optionsReverse = list(refine = TRUE, gradtol = 1e-3))
controls(x, name = "optionsReverse") <- list(refine = FALSE)   # the grid of the value pass again
```

| entry | controls |
|---|---|
| `refine` | `TRUE`: each sweep step passes the error test of the solve, else is redone in substeps |
| `gradtol` | absolute tolerance for the share of each step in the gradient |

Under `refine`, value and `chi2` of the reverse objective include the change from the computed to
the refined trajectory, the attribute `correction`
([Methods > Accuracy of a reverse gradient](methods-sensitivities.html#accuracy-of-a-reverse-gradient)).

## Forward over reverse

The exact Hessian without second-order sensitivities, one column per parameter from the backward
sweep ([Methods > Forward over reverse](methods-sensitivities.html#forward-over-reverse)). Build with
`derivMode = c("forward", "reverse", "forward-reverse")` and call with
`sweep = "reverse", deriv2 = TRUE`. FOCEI in [Nonlinear mixed-effects models](guide-nlme.html)
uses the same sweeps for directional second derivatives.

## ODE backends

`odemodel(backend = )` selects the solver; the function objects above are the same, `Xs()`
dispatches on the model class.

| backend | solver | forward | fwd/fwd | reverse | fwd/rev | use |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `"cppDE"` (default) | C++: BDF/NDF, Adams, Rosenbrock, Tsitouras | duals | `deriv2` | discrete adjoint | yes | all models |
| `"Sundials"` | CVODES, `cppDE::cvode()` | CVODES | no | CVODES ASA | no | first-order derivatives |
| `"deSolve"` | `lsodes`, cOde | sens. equations | no | no | no | dMod models |

See cppDE on [stepping](https://dmodverse.github.io/cppDE/articles/methods-stepping.html),
[CVODES](https://dmodverse.github.io/cppDE/articles/methods-cvode.html) and
[benchmarks](https://dmodverse.github.io/cppDE/articles/benchmarks.html) against CVODES.

## Costs on the guide model

`sensitivities.R` rebuilds the chain of [Setting up models](guide-model.html) with all directions
and evaluates the data term at the best fit of [Optimization](guide-optimization.html):

```{r reversechain, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r}
s <- readRDS("results/sensitivities.rds")
```

Reverse and forward gradients agree:

```{r gradients, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r}
max(abs(s$gradients$forward - s$gradients$reverse)) / max(abs(s$gradients$forward))
```

within the solver tolerances, since the sweep without `refine` runs on the grid of the value
pass. Seconds per evaluation, minimum of ten:

```{r cost, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r}
s$timing
```

A reverse gradient costs a few values, a forward gradient one solve with a tangent per
parameter, forward over reverse about
`r round(s$timing[["forward-reverse"]] / s$timing[["forward"]], 1)` forward
gradients. Forward over forward, measured once:

```{r forwardforward, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r}
c(seconds = s$forwardForward, s$memory)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
peakText <- if (s$memory[["forwardForward"]] > s$memory[["before"]] + 0.05) {
  sprintf("raises the peak memory of the process from %.1f to %.1f GB", s$memory[["before"]],
          s$memory[["forwardForward"]])
} else sprintf("leaves the peak memory of the process at %.1f GB", s$memory[["before"]])
```

It takes `r round(s$forwardForward / s$timing[["forward-reverse"]])`
times as long as forward over reverse and `r peakText`;
for this model it is a check, not a method. Both Hessians agree up to the solver error:

```{r hessians, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r}
max(abs(s$forwardForwardHessian[rownames(s$exact), colnames(s$exact)] - s$exact)) / max(abs(s$exact))
```

Eigenvalues of exact and Gauss-Newton Hessian at the best fit:

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
eig <- data.frame(rank = rep(seq_len(nrow(s$hessians)), 2),
                  value = c(s$hessians$exact, s$hessians$gaussNewton),
                  Hessian = rep(c("exact", "Gauss-Newton"), each = nrow(s$hessians)))
ggplot2::ggplot(eig, ggplot2::aes(rank, value, color = Hessian)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point() +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(trans = scales::pseudo_log_trans(sigma = 1e-3, base = 10),
                              breaks = c(-1e-1, 0, 1e-2, 1, 1e2, 1e4)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "rank", y = "eigenvalue") +
  theme_dMod()
```

They agree in the large eigenvalues, the well-determined directions. The smallest eigenvalue is
`r signif(min(s$hessians$exact), 2)` for the exact Hessian and
`r signif(min(s$hessians$gaussNewton), 2)` for Gauss-Newton. The model estimates the standard
deviations of the imaging readouts, and with an error model Gauss-Newton can be indefinite
([Gauss-Newton with an error model](methods-sensitivities.html#gauss-newton-with-an-error-model)).
In the flat directions the Hessian sources of [Optimization](guide-optimization.html) take
different steps.

Reference: `odemodel()`, `Xs()`, `Y()`, `P()`, `Pimpl()`, `normL2()`, `controls()`, `trust()`
